guide.title: The Second Coming Guided Plan
guide.description: A 5-day guided plan for William Butler Yeats's The Second Coming.

poem.title: The Second Coming
poem.author: William Butler Yeats
poem.text:
Turning and turning in the widening gyre
The falcon cannot hear the falconer;
Things fall apart; the centre cannot hold;
Mere anarchy is loosed upon the world,

The blood-dimmed tide is loosed, and everywhere
The ceremony of innocence is drowned;
The best lack all conviction, while the worst
Are full of passionate intensity.

Surely some revelation is at hand;
Surely the Second Coming is at hand.
The Second Coming! Hardly are those words out
When a vast image out of Spiritus Mundi
Troubles my sight: somewhere in sands of the desert

A shape with lion body and the head of a man,
A gaze blank and pitiless as the sun,
Is moving its slow thighs, while all about it
Reel shadows of the indignant desert birds.

The darkness drops again; but now I know
That twenty centuries of stony sleep
Were vexed to nightmare by a rocking cradle,
And what rough beast, its hour come round at last,
Slouches towards Bethlehem to be born?

pages.title: A Poem That Begins in Motion
pages.bodyMarkdown:
Yeats wrote this poem after the First World War, during a period when Europe had become very good at disproving its own faith in progress. It is only twenty-two lines long, but it sounds as if it has looked at a whole century and found the floor giving way.

You will learn it over five days. Today is the first turn of the wheel: the widening spiral, the lost signal, and the moment when the poem says plainly what it fears.

pages.title: After the Centre Gives Way
pages.bodyMarkdown:
Yeats was not writing from a quiet room outside history. The war had ended in 1918. Ireland was moving through revolution and violence. The old empires looked damaged, and the new political certainties did not look much cleaner. Yeats had spent years thinking about history as a pattern of cycles, not as a neat ladder upwards.

That is why the poem begins with a "gyre," a spiral that widens as it turns. The image is abstract, but it immediately becomes practical: a falcon has flown too far out to hear the person who trained it. Order has not been argued away. It has drifted out of range.

pages.title: Too Far to Hear
pages.bodyMarkdown:
"Turning and turning" gives you repetition before it gives you explanation. The phrase circles in the mouth, and the line itself refuses to arrive quickly. Yeats makes you feel the motion before you are told what kind of motion it is.

The falcon image is exact. A trained falcon should return to the falconer. Here, it cannot even hear him. The disaster is not loud at first. It is distance. Command, training, memory, and trust are all still present, but the connection between them has failed.

pages.title: The Sentence Breaks Open
pages.bodyMarkdown:
The poem is written in loose blank verse, but it does not move with calm conversational ease. The first four lines keep pressing forward, each phrase adding another loss. There is no rhyme to settle the ear. The lines feel controlled and unstable at once.

"Mere anarchy" does not mean a small amount of anarchy. "Mere" means pure, absolute, stripped of disguise. Yeats is not describing ordinary disorder. He is imagining disorder released as a force in its own right.

pages.title: Things Fall Apart
pages.bodyMarkdown:
"Things fall apart" has become famous because it is so plain. After the gyre and the falcon, Yeats suddenly gives you a sentence that sounds almost blunt. Its force comes from how little it decorates the fact.

Then the line tightens: "the centre cannot hold." A centre normally gathers things around it. It gives shape to movement. If it cannot hold, the problem is not only at the edges. The governing middle has failed, and the poem has only just begun.

pages.title: Violence Without Ceremony
pages.bodyMarkdown:
Yeats had seen public violence become part of ordinary political weather. The Easter Rising of 1916, the executions that followed, the Russian Revolution, the First World War, and the violence in Ireland after it all sit behind this poem. Not as footnotes to decode every line, but as the pressure in the room.

The phrase "ceremony of innocence" is strange because innocence usually sounds natural, not ceremonial. Yeats makes innocence feel like something society has to enact and protect. Once the tide comes in, that delicate public ritual is drowned.

pages.title: Loosed Upon the World
pages.bodyMarkdown:
"The blood-dimmed tide" turns violence into water. That makes it worse, not cleaner. A tide does not argue with you. It rises, spreads, covers, and makes distinctions hard to see.

Yeats repeats "loosed" from the previous line of the poem. The repetition matters for memory, but it also matters morally. Anarchy is loosed; the tide is loosed. The verb suggests something chained, penned in, or restrained until now. The poem hears history as a gate opening.

pages.title: The Line Everyone Quotes
pages.bodyMarkdown:
"The best lack all conviction, while the worst / Are full of passionate intensity" has had a long afterlife because it is brutally portable. It can be applied too easily, which is both its strength and its danger.

In the poem, the line is not a clever complaint about bad manners or shallow politics. It comes after anarchy, blood, and drowned innocence. Yeats is describing a public world where hesitation belongs to the decent, and energy belongs to the destructive.

pages.title: Best and Worst
pages.bodyMarkdown:
The last two lines are balanced almost like a scale: "The best" on one side, "the worst" on the other. But the balance is sick. The best are defined by absence. They "lack." The worst are defined by fullness.

"Passionate intensity" is not condemned because passion is always bad. Yeats is more exact than that. The phrase becomes frightening because it belongs to "the worst." Feeling has detached from judgment, and conviction has detached from goodness.

pages.title: Revelation and the World Mind
pages.bodyMarkdown:
Yeats was fascinated by occult systems, symbols, cycles, and hidden correspondences. After his marriage to Georgie Hyde-Lees in 1917, he began receiving what he believed were messages through her automatic writing. He later shaped some of these ideas into *A Vision*, his dense and eccentric book about history's cycles.

"Spiritus Mundi" means something like the spirit or mind of the world. In this poem, the image does not feel privately invented. It feels as if it rises from a shared storehouse of human symbols, older and less polite than ordinary thought.

pages.title: Surely, Surely
pages.bodyMarkdown:
The repetition of "Surely" sounds like self-persuasion. The word claims confidence, but saying it twice makes the confidence feel pressured. The speaker is trying to make a pattern appear.

"The Second Coming" is a Christian phrase for the return of Christ and the fulfilment of history. Yeats writes it, then immediately breaks the expected frame: "Hardly are those words out." The line makes the speaker sound interrupted by his own vision. The poem does not calmly introduce the image. It is seized by it.

pages.title: A Broken Expectation
pages.bodyMarkdown:
The title of the poem invites a Christian expectation before the first line even begins. You hear "The Second Coming" and expect return, judgment, and perhaps restoration. Yeats uses that expectation, but he does not satisfy it.

The vision begins in the desert, not in a church or a city. That matters. The desert can be biblical, but it can also be pre-biblical, stripped down, sun-struck, and inhuman. The poem moves towards a religious image by entering a place where human comfort has very little authority.

pages.title: Troubles My Sight
pages.bodyMarkdown:
"A vast image" is carefully vague. Yeats lets scale arrive before definition. The speaker sees something large enough to overwhelm ordinary sight, but not yet clear enough to name.

The phrase "Troubles my sight" is stronger than "appears to me." The vision does not simply enter the eye. It disturbs the act of seeing. By the end of today's chunk, you are suspended just before the creature comes into focus.

pages.title: The Sphinx Without Mercy
pages.bodyMarkdown:
The creature recalls the sphinx: lion body, human head, desert setting. That association brings Egypt, riddles, age, and monument into the poem without needing to name them. Yeats lets the old shape do its work.

But this is not a museum object. It is moving. That is the line's shock. Something ancient, stony, and symbolic has entered time again, and the birds around it are not peaceful witnesses.

pages.title: Blank and Pitiless
pages.bodyMarkdown:
"A shape" is an oddly bare phrase for such a memorable creature. Yeats does not give it a name. Naming would make it easier to file away. "Shape" keeps it present and unfinished.

The gaze is "blank and pitiless as the sun." The simile is exact because the sun is not cruel in a human way. It simply shines without mercy, without preference, without noticing what it burns. The creature's face has that same absence of inward softness.

pages.title: A Slow Body
pages.bodyMarkdown:
The phrase "moving its slow thighs" has always unsettled people, and rightly. It makes the symbolic creature bodily. The poem does not let it remain a decorative emblem of apocalypse. It has weight. It has legs. It advances.

The desert birds are "indignant," a surprisingly social word. They seem offended or disturbed by the creature's motion, as if even the desert has rules that this thing violates.

pages.title: Slow Thighs, Reel Shadows
pages.bodyMarkdown:
The sound of "slow thighs" drags. Both words are heavy with long vowels, and the phrase makes the line move with the creature. The poem's music does not merely describe slowness. It performs it.

Then the movement around the creature changes: "Reel shadows." The birds are reduced to shadows, and their motion is dizzy, circular, unstable. The creature moves slowly; the world around it spins.

pages.title: Twenty Centuries
pages.bodyMarkdown:
"Twenty centuries" points back to the age of Christianity, roughly the time since the birth of Christ. Yeats imagines that whole era not as settled triumph, but as a long sleep that can be disturbed.

The "rocking cradle" is one of the poem's quiet cruelties. A cradle should soothe a child. Here, it vexes the old shape into nightmare. The image of birth remains, but comfort has gone out of it.

pages.title: Darkness, Then Knowledge
pages.bodyMarkdown:
"The darkness drops again" sounds like a curtain falling. The vision has ended. But Yeats adds "but now I know," and that phrase changes everything. The speaker has not merely seen an image. He believes the image has interpreted history.

"Stony sleep" belongs to the sphinx-like creature, but it also belongs to the long dead weight of an age. Stone suggests monument, burial, and endurance. Sleep suggests something capable of waking. The phrase holds both at once.

pages.title: Bethlehem Reimagined
pages.bodyMarkdown:
Bethlehem is the place of Christ's birth, so the final line pulls the whole poem back into the language of nativity. But the expected child has been replaced by a "rough beast." Yeats keeps the sacred map and changes what is travelling across it.

That is why the ending feels so cold. The poem does not say that nothing is coming. Something is coming. The fear is that history's next birth may answer an old religious form with an opposite spirit.

pages.title: Slouches Towards Bethlehem
pages.bodyMarkdown:
"Rough beast" refuses grandeur. The creature is not called a king, god, angel, or demon. "Rough" makes it coarse, unfinished, and physical. "Beast" strips away the human head's possible dignity.

Then comes "Slouches." It is one of the great final verbs in English poetry because it is so ugly and slow. The thing does not march, descend, or blaze. It slouches. The birth it moves towards is not sudden. It is inevitable enough to take its time.
